newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Rebuilding of S.Lanka oil tanks to start Jan 98.
newsitem.headline: Rebuilding of S.Lanka oil tanks to start Jan 98.

text.p: Reconstruction of Sri Lankan oil tanks blown up by Tamil Tiger rebels in 1995 is likely to start in January 1998, state oil firm Ceylon Petroleum Corp (CPC) said on Wednesday.
CPC Chairman Anil Obeyesekere told Reuters that 11 foreign companies had been short-listed for the contract, which is expected to be worth more than $50 million.
He declined to identify the shortlisted companies but industry sources said they included firms from India, Japan, China, South Korea, Italy and Singapore.
Obeyesekere said tenders to build the oil tanks, at Orugodawatte and Kolonnawa just north of the capital Colombo, would close on August 26.
Offers would then be scrutinised by a technical evaluation committee and a decision would be announced two or three months later, he said.

"We are virtually on track but I think the award for the contract should be made some time in October...or November. Then the contractor has to come on the ground. Work will commence some time in January of next year," Obeyesekere said in an interview.
"We are hoping, if everything is on schedule, that those will be the dates," he added.
A total of 16 crude and oil product tanks were destroyed or damaged by Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) guerrillas in a raid in October 1995.
The LTTE is fighting a 14-year-old war with the Sri Lankan government for a separate homeland for the minority Tamils in the Indian Ocean island's north and east.
A CPC official said in May that construction of the tanks was likely to start in September.
Obeyesekere said CPC hoped to have the tanks completed by November 1999.
The tanks would have the capacity to hold 105,000 tonnes of oil products, of which 40,000 tonnes would be for gas oil, and a further 120,000 tonnes of crude oil.
He said CPC had arranged an in-principle loan of 1.6 billion rupees ($27.2 million) for construction of the tanks but would not finalise the contract until the tender date had passed.
"The money is available but we don't want to raise the money while the bids are open," he said. "We have arranged for it from local funding...from local banks."
The balance of the cost of the tanks -- around $24 million -- will come from a loan from the Asian Development Bank (ADB). ($1=58.8 rupees)
